raw_evidence.label: First 3-nation, 16-city World Cup
raw_evidence.content: The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the first to be co-hosted by three countries — the United States, Canada and Mexico — and the first to be spread across 16 host cities: 11 in the U.S., 3 in Mexico, and 2 in Canada. It is also the first 48-team, 104-match edition, expanded from 32 teams and 64 matches. The U.S. hosts 78 matches (including everything from the quarterfinals onward), while Canada and Mexico host 13 each. This continental scale — from Vancouver and Seattle in the cool Pacific Northwest to Miami in subtropical Florida to Mexico City at 2,200 m altitude — is the geographic spine of the tournament and the reason climate varies so wildly between venues.

raw_evidence.label: Feels-like spread of 17.1C across venues
raw_evidence.content: Ranking all 16 venues by average apparent (feels-like) high temperature in the tournament window reveals an enormous spread. Houston tops it at 38.6C feels-like, with Dallas/Arlington at 38.3C, Miami at 36.9C and Monterrey at 36.2C. At the cool end sit Vancouver (21.5C), Seattle (23.1C) and Mexico City (24.3C, tempered by its altitude). The gap between the hottest and coolest venue is 17.1C — the difference between dangerous heat-stress conditions and a mild spring afternoon, within the same tournament.
raw_evidence.code:
hm = []
for r in wx:
    score = cnt[r["stadium"]] * fnum(r,"avg_apparent_high_c")
    hm.append([r["city"], cnt[r["stadium"]], round(fnum(r,"avg_apparent_high_c"),1), round(score,1)])
hm.sort(key=lambda x: x[3], reverse=True)
for city, m, fl, sc in hm:
    print(f"{sc:>7.1f}  {city:<22} {m} matches x {fl}C")
# share of "hot football": matches at feels-like >= 34C
hot_venues = [r for r in wx if fnum(r,"avg_apparent_high_c") >= 34]
hot_matches = sum(cnt[r["stadium"]] for r in hot_venues)
print(f"matches at venues with feels-like >= 34C: {hot_matches} of 104 = {round(100*hot_matches/104,1)}%")
fifapro6 = {"Atlanta Stadium","Dallas Stadium","Houston Stadium","Kansas City Stadium","Miami Stadium","Estadio Monterrey"}
raw_evidence.output:
38.6C feels (33.5C air) hum 76.5% Houston / NRG Stadium
 38.3C feels (34.9C air) hum 61.6% Arlington / AT&T Stadium
 36.9C feels (31.0C air) hum 82.9% Miami Gardens
 36.2C feels Monterrey
 ...
 23.1C Seattle
 21.5C Vancouver
feels-like spread: 38.6C (Houston) to 21.5C (Vancouver) = 17.1C

raw_evidence.label: First 3-nation, 16-city World Cup
raw_evidence.content: The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the first to be co-hosted by three countries — the United States, Canada and Mexico — and the first to be spread across 16 host cities: 11 in the U.S., 3 in Mexico, and 2 in Canada. It is also the first 48-team, 104-match edition, expanded from 32 teams and 64 matches. The U.S. hosts 78 matches (including everything from the quarterfinals onward), while Canada and Mexico host 13 each. This continental scale — from Vancouver and Seattle in the cool Pacific Northwest to Miami in subtropical Florida to Mexico City at 2,200 m altitude — is the geographic spine of the tournament and the reason climate varies so wildly between venues.

raw_evidence.label: Climate data is historical typical, not a forecast
raw_evidence.content: The weather figures used throughout this story come from the Open-Meteo historical archive, averaged over the 11 June – 19 July window across 2021–2024 for each venue's coordinates (CC BY 4.0). They describe the TYPICAL climate a venue experiences during the tournament window — not a 2026 forecast for any specific match date. 'Apparent temperature' (feels-like) approximates a heat index by combining air temperature with humidity, wind and radiation, which is why humid Houston and Miami feel hotter than their raw air temperature alone. This caveat must be stated plainly in the blog: these are climatological expectations, the loaded dice, not a prediction of any one day.

raw_evidence.label: First 3-nation, 16-city World Cup
raw_evidence.content: The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the first to be co-hosted by three countries — the United States, Canada and Mexico — and the first to be spread across 16 host cities: 11 in the U.S., 3 in Mexico, and 2 in Canada. It is also the first 48-team, 104-match edition, expanded from 32 teams and 64 matches. The U.S. hosts 78 matches (including everything from the quarterfinals onward), while Canada and Mexico host 13 each. This continental scale — from Vancouver and Seattle in the cool Pacific Northwest to Miami in subtropical Florida to Mexico City at 2,200 m altitude — is the geographic spine of the tournament and the reason climate varies so wildly between venues.

raw_evidence.label: Schedule window and three regional clusters
raw_evidence.content: The tournament runs 39 days, from 11 June to 19 July 2026 — longer than the 32-day 2014 and 2018 editions — with 72 group-stage matches and 24 knockout matches. To limit punishing travel across a continent, FIFA grouped the 16 host cities into three regional clusters: a Western Region (Vancouver, Seattle, San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles), a Central Region (Guadalajara, Mexico City, Monterrey, Houston, Dallas, Kansas City), and an Eastern Region (Atlanta, Miami, Toronto, Boston, Philadelphia, New York/New Jersey). Even so, the spread covers four time zones and thousands of kilometres, and the climate the clusters experience in mid-summer is dramatically different.

raw_evidence.content: The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the first to be co-hosted by three countries — the United States, Canada and Mexico — and the first to be spread across 16 host cities: 11 in the U.S., 3 in Mexico, and 2 in Canada. raw_evidence.label: Heat is the headline player-welfare concern
raw_evidence.content: Heat is the defining off-pitch story of the 2026 World Cup. FIFPRO, the global players' union, has identified six venues — Atlanta, Dallas, Houston, Kansas City and Miami in the U.S. plus Monterrey in Mexico — as posing an 'extremely high risk' of heat-stress injury to players, with three more rated 'very high risk.' A staging of the tournament in June–July across the southern U.S. and Mexico puts it squarely in the hottest part of the year for those cities. The concern is not abstract: it shapes how the schedule's afternoon kickoffs in those cities should be read.

raw_evidence.label: FIFA vs FIFPRO WBGT threshold dispute
raw_evidence.content: There is an open dispute between FIFA and FIFPRO over how hot is too hot. FIFPRO recommends postponing play when the wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) reaches 28°C (82.4°F); FIFA does not consider postponement until WBGT exceeds 32°C (89.6°F). Around five matches could plausibly reach the 28°C WBGT level. A group of health, sports-performance and climate experts publicly called FIFA's heat guidelines 'impossible to justify.' FIFA's confirmed mitigation for 2026 is mandatory three-minute hydration breaks in each half — which medical experts say does not go far enough. This is the genuine controversy a weather-focused story must engage with honestly.

raw_evidence.label: 2025 Club World Cup was the heat dress rehearsal
raw_evidence.content: The 2025 FIFA Club World Cup, staged in the U.S. the summer before, was widely seen as a stress test for 2026. Players battled extreme heat — temperatures peaked at around 104°F (40°C) for Benfica v Bayern Munich in Charlotte, and players including Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham described the conditions as extremely difficult. After FIFPRO intervened early in that tournament, FIFA lowered the cooling-break WBGT threshold to 82.4°F and added extra water, ice and towels pitchside — a departure from its standard 32°C policy. The Club World Cup is the empirical precedent that makes the 2026 heat concern concrete rather than speculative.

raw_evidence.label: FIFA vs FIFPRO WBGT threshold dispute
raw_evidence.content: There is an open dispute between FIFA and FIFPRO over how hot is too hot. FIFPRO recommends postponing play when the wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) reaches 28°C (82.4°F); FIFA does not consider postponement until WBGT exceeds 32°C (89.6°F). Around five matches could plausibly reach the 28°C WBGT level. A group of health, sports-performance and climate experts publicly called FIFA's heat guidelines 'impossible to justify.' FIFA's confirmed mitigation for 2026 is mandatory three-minute hydration breaks in each half — which medical experts say does not go far enough. This is the genuine controversy a weather-focused story must engage with honestly.

raw_evidence.label: 2025 Club World Cup was the heat dress rehearsal
raw_evidence.content: The 2025 FIFA Club World Cup, staged in the U.S. the summer before, was widely seen as a stress test for 2026. Players battled extreme heat — temperatures peaked at around 104°F (40°C) for Benfica v Bayern Munich in Charlotte, and players including Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham described the conditions as extremely difficult. After FIFPRO intervened early in that tournament, FIFA lowered the cooling-break WBGT threshold to 82.4°F and added extra water, ice and towels pitchside — a departure from its standard 32°C policy. The Club World Cup is the empirical precedent that makes the 2026 heat concern concrete rather than speculative.

raw_evidence.label: Roofs and air conditioning mitigate — partly
raw_evidence.content: Not every hot venue is equally exposed. Several 2026 stadiums have roofs and climate control: Mercedes-Benz Stadium (Atlanta), AT&T Stadium (Dallas) and NRG Stadium (Houston) offer full climate control, and BC Place (Vancouver) has a roof. FIFA President Gianni Infantino has said roofed stadiums will be used for daytime matches: 'we have stadiums with roofs, and we will definitely use these stadiums during the day.' The crucial caveat: BC Place's roof will be OPEN for all 2026 matches because FIFA requires natural sunlight on the grass pitch, and the final venue MetLife has no roof at all. So a fair weather story must note that the worst raw heat numbers (Dallas, Houston, Atlanta) are partly buffered by AC, while some exposed venues are not — the climate data is the hazard, the roof is the mitigation.

This tension — TV windows versus the thermometer — is the practical bridge between the schedule data and the climate data.

raw_evidence.label: Four climate tribes: brutal, dry-hot, warm, mild
raw_evidence.content: Plotting feels-like high against humidity sorts the 16 venues into four tribes. Three are 'brutal' — hot AND humid: Houston (38.6C, 76%), Miami (36.9C, 83%) and Atlanta (34.1C, 73%). Six are 'warm', and five are genuinely 'mild' (feels-like at or below 27C): Mexico City, Toronto, Vancouver, Seattle and Santa Clara. The brutal tribe is the player-welfare hotspot; the mild tribe is where European players will feel most at home.

raw_evidence.label: Four climate tribes: brutal, dry-hot, warm, mild
raw_evidence.content: Plotting feels-like high against humidity sorts the 16 venues into four tribes. Three are 'brutal' — hot AND humid: Houston (38.6C, 76%), Miami (36.9C, 83%) and Atlanta (34.1C, 73%). Two are 'dry-hot' — fierce air temperature but lower humidity, where evaporative cooling and roofs help: Dallas (38.3C, 62%) and Monterrey (36.2C, 64%). Six are 'warm', and five are genuinely 'mild' (feels-like at or below 27C): Mexico City, Toronto, Vancouver, Seattle and Santa Clara. The brutal tribe is the player-welfare hotspot; the mild tribe is where European players will feel most at home.

raw_evidence.label: Opener in Mexico City, final at MetLife
raw_evidence.content: The opening match is at Estadio Azteca in Mexico City on 11 June 2026 — a stadium sitting at roughly 2,200 m of altitude, the highest venue in the tournament. raw_evidence.label: FIFA vs FIFPRO WBGT threshold dispute
raw_evidence.content: There is an open dispute between FIFA and FIFPRO over how hot is too hot. FIFPRO recommends postponing play when the wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) reaches 28°C (82.4°F); FIFA does not consider postponement until WBGT exceeds 32°C (89.6°F). Around five matches could plausibly reach the 28°C WBGT level. A group of health, sports-performance and climate experts publicly called FIFA's heat guidelines 'impossible to justify.' FIFA's confirmed mitigation for 2026 is mandatory three-minute hydration breaks in each half — which medical experts say does not go far enough. This is the genuine controversy a weather-focused story must engage with honestly.

raw_evidence.label: Climate data is historical typical, not a forecast
raw_evidence.content: The weather figures used throughout this story come from the Open-Meteo historical archive, averaged over the 11 June – 19 July window across 2021–2024 for each venue's coordinates (CC BY 4.0). They describe the TYPICAL climate a venue experiences during the tournament window — not a 2026 forecast for any specific match date. 'Apparent temperature' (feels-like) approximates a heat index by combining air temperature with humidity, wind and radiation, which is why humid Houston and Miami feel hotter than their raw air temperature alone. This caveat must be stated plainly in the blog: these are climatological expectations, the loaded dice, not a prediction of any one day.

raw_evidence.label: A third of all matches in dangerous heat
raw_evidence.content: Combining match load with climate shows where the most football is played in the most heat. Weighting each venue's matches by its feels-like high, Dallas tops the 'heat exposure' index (9 matches x 38.3C), followed by Atlanta, Houston and Miami. Crucially, 35 of the 104 matches (33.7%) are at venues whose typical feels-like high is 34C or more, and 41 matches (39.4%) fall at the six venues FIFPRO flagged as 'extremely high risk' for heat-stress injury. So roughly four in ten World Cup matches are scheduled into the climate band that prompted the player-welfare alarm.
raw_evidence.code:
# ---------- ana_06: rain exposure ----------
print("=== ana_06 ===")
rain = sorted(wx, key=lambda r: fnum(r,"rainy_day_share"), reverse=True)
rain_rows = []
for r in rain:
    rain_rows.append([r["city"], round(fnum(r,"rainy_day_share")*100), round(fnum(r,"avg_precip_mm_per_day"),1), cnt[r["stadium"]]])
    print(f"{fnum(r,'rainy_day_share')*100:>5.0f}% wet days  {fnum(r,'avg_precip_mm_per_day'):>4.1f}mm/day  {r['city']}")

# ---------- ana_07: altitude ----------
print("=== ana_07 ===")
alt = sorted(wx, key=lambda r: fnum(r,"elevation_m"), reverse=True)
alt_rows = []
for r in alt:
    alt_rows.append([r["city"], int(fnum(r,"elevation_m")), cnt[r["stadium"]]])
    print(f"{int(fnum(r,'elevation_m')):>5}m  {r['city']}  ({r['venue']})")
